text:
Relevant work supports learning temporal relevance inside attention. [TiSASRec](https://jiachengli1995.github.io/files/wsdm20.pdf) combines positions with pairwise historical time-interval embeddings in attention keys and values; its historical interval matrix requires no next-event timestamp. Borrow that mechanism while retaining bidirectional masked-target BERT4Rec. More directly, [Ti-CoRe (2026)](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cpe.70585) introduces a time-interval-aware T-BERT encoder, although its accessible abstract does not establish how prediction-time timestamps are handled.

Recent work also motivates adaptive persistence: [TLSTSRec (online 2024; volume 2025)](https://doi.org/10.3233/ida-240051) learns temporal representations and adaptive long/short-term fusion. A [2026 BERT4Rec session-enhancement paper](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01554-z) combines content relevance, continuous temporal decay and gated representations. These offer architectural ideas, but their reported results do not establish gains under the pinned Amazon benchmark.

Practical hypothesis, inferred from these mechanisms: add per-head learned biases over log-bucketed historical gaps and relative positions within the existing BERT4Rec network; optionally learn content-conditioned decay so older relevant items can retain attention. For the appended mask, use a dedicated temporal relation or ages anchored to the latest observed interaction—never the unknown target timestamp. Keep masked-target training and one jointly trained checkpoint per category. Compare against the uniform-cutoff control using identical seeds, budgets, splits and macro validation HR@10; include a position-only ablation to isolate timestamp value. Conflicting branch-allocation documentation is unavailable here, so its resolution and any experimental advantage remain unverified.
